record.question:
A company is migrating a Java application and MongoDB database to AWS. It must preserve the application's code and general architecture, although deployment and connection settings can change. A completed compatibility test confirms that the application's commands, drivers and behavior work with the selected Amazon DocumentDB version. The application and database must remain recoverable after a single Availability Zone fails, with database compute already available in another zone.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the Java application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB across multiple Availability Zones. Migrate to an instance-based DocumentDB cluster with a primary and at least one replica in another Availability Zone.
Containerize the Java application with App2Container and deploy it to a multi-AZ EKS cluster. Replace MongoDB with DynamoDB tables.
Deploy the Java application through Elastic Beanstalk across multiple Availability Zones. Replace MongoDB with an Aurora MySQL cluster and replicas.

Run the Java application in a multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB. Use a DocumentDB cluster with one primary instance and no replicas, relying on its replicated storage for database compute failover.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct under the stated compatibility test. The application tier spans zones, and a DocumentDB replica in a different zone provides an existing instance that can be promoted when the primary fails. The application must reconnect and retry through the appropriate cluster endpoint during failover.

<<2>> changes the database API and data model to DynamoDB, requiring application changes despite the container tooling. <<3>> similarly changes the database to a relational engine; a managed Java deployment does not remove that incompatibility. <<4>> confuses storage durability with compute availability. Replicated storage does not create a running replica in another zone, and a single-instance cluster must attempt to recreate its primary after failure.

DocumentDB compatibility is workload-specific, not a guarantee for every MongoDB application. Validate supported APIs, operators, indexes, drivers and behavior for the selected version. The scenario explicitly supplies that evidence; without it, a no-code-change migration to DocumentDB would not be established.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/documentdb/latest/devguide/mongo-apis.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/documentdb/latest/devguide/failover.html

diagram_alt: An existing replica in another Availability Zone is promoted after a primary failure, and the application reconnects to the promoted instance.

sources.supports: DocumentDB implements a defined set of MongoDB-compatible APIs and has compatibility differences.
Replica promotion provides failover, while a single-instance cluster must recreate its primary.

editorial_notes: Made the existing DocumentDB compatibility assessment central and stated that deployment settings may change without code changes.
Distinguished cross-AZ storage replication from pre-provisioned replica compute and removed implied zero-interruption guarantees.
